content:
Meeting header: 2026-09-23 15:00 UTC | Duration: 48m
Attendees: Liam (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (Argentia CTO), Ruth Park (ML Eng), Omar Zayed (Infra), Leah Kim (PM)
Summary: Weekly POC sync — bench readout comparing Redwood inference runtime vs incumbent baseline (CloudX). Reviewed p50/p95 latency deltas, throughput at target QPS, routing and fallback playbook, and next steps for long-tail prompt testing and pricing. Some transcription artifacts and speaker overlaps.
Topics: bench numbers, routing decision (dedicated vs hosted), KV cache behavior, quantization/accuracy tradeoffs, SLOs and pilot cutover timeline
Action items (rough): Priya to run extended head-to-head, Omar to share logs/access, Liam to send pricing

00:00:00 Speaker 1 (Liam): Alright, thanks everyone for carving out time. Uh, quick check — can you all hear me?
00:00:06 Speaker 2 (Carlos): Yep, loud and clear. Thanks, Liam.
00:00:10 Speaker 1 (Liam): Great. Today we want to walk through the sprint 4 bench readout — I'll hand to Priya for the numbers and then we'll go into routing decisions.
00:00:20 Speaker 3 (Priya): Cool thanks. So I ran the head-to-head with the set we agreed — 10k requests, a 60/40 short-to-long prompt mix, token limits set to 256/1024 respectively. Baseline is CloudX endpoint (their v3-small), Redwood ran on a dedicated 4-slot pool with our quantized 4-bit runtime.
00:00:42 Speaker 3 (Priya): High level: p50 latency delta is about -23% in favor of Redwood — baseline p50 is around 210ms, Redwood 162ms. p95 delta is larger: baseline p95 ~620ms, Redwood p95 ~385ms, so about -38% which is pretty meaningful for tail-sensitive UX.
00:01:04 Speaker 4 (Ruth): Wait, Ruth here — is that with prefix caching enabled? We saw big wins earlier with K-V cache — sorry K-V, K-V — kind of cache.
00:01:12 Speaker 3 (Priya): Yes, good call. For the short prompts the KV cache hit rate was ~48% given the synthetic dataset; for the long prompts cache doesn't help as much. I ran a second pass with cache disabled to isolate kernel perf; without cache p95 was closer but still ~20% better on Redwood.
00:01:31 Speaker 5 (Omar): Omar — curious about concurrency. What QPS were you driving and how did batching behave?
00:01:36 Speaker 3 (Priya): We ramped to sustained 120 QPS at 8 concurrent workers, observed average batch size of 6 tokens per step. Batching and our continuous batching scheduler kept latency stable; throughput peak was about 1.1k tokens/sec across the pool. Baseline peaked lower — around 800 tokens/sec before latency degraded.
00:01:56 Speaker 2 (Carlos): Is the baseline run on their latest optimized runtime or our re-run of their public endpoint?
00:02:02 Speaker 3 (Priya): We used a customer-reported configuration — CloudX managed endpoint with their default optimization flags. Not their internal perf-tune. We matched sequence lengths and request patterns. We also noted CloudX had larger variance on noisy tails.
00:02:17 Speaker 6 (Leah): Leah here — for the p95 improvements, are we seeing any accuracy regressions with the quantized model? We can't sacrifice NLU quality.
00:02:26 Speaker 3 (Priya): Good question. We ran a 500-sample eval set — overall intent accuracy delta within +/-0.6% which is within noise. A few failure modes on rare entity extraction for longer prompts, so we flagged 4 prompts that dropped confidence. I'll include that in the artifact list.
00:02:45 Speaker 1 (Liam): And to be transparent, we applied our 4-bit quant profile plus mild bias-correction on the attention kernels. That explains some of the speed gains.
00:02:54 Speaker 4 (Ruth): Are those bias fixes reversible? Like if we need full fp16 we can run that?
00:02:58 Speaker 3 (Priya): Absolutely — we can switch to fp16 in the dedicated pool, you'll see about +12% latency and ~20% higher cost but sometimes needed for certain evals.
00:03:09 Speaker 5 (Omar): For our staging traffic we want to run a skewed mix — 85% short, 15% long — can you simulate that?
00:03:15 Speaker 3 (Priya): Yep we can. Priya: noted — will run that skew and surface p50/p95 and tail regressions.
00:03:22 Speaker 2 (Carlos): Also curious about fallbacks — if we overflow the dedicated pool, how do we route? Do we go to hosted Redwood or to CloudX?
00:03:30 Speaker 1 (Liam): We can set policy. Typical playbook: primary route to dedicated, fallback to hosted Redwood in same region for latency parity, and as a last resort to incumbent if that's mandatory for data locality. We generally advise against routing to incumbent since that complicates tracing and increases unit cost.
00:03:47 Speaker 6 (Leah): What about authentication and logs? We need traceability for PHI masking.
00:03:53 Speaker 3 (Priya): Dedicated includes token-level tracing and optional audit logs pushed to your S3 or SIEM via our connectors. We also integrate with KMS for key rotation. We noted Argenta (sic) earlier — sorry — Argentia — sits on AWS — so we tested KMS vault integration.
00:04:12 Speaker 4 (Ruth): Appreciate the spelling help, haha.
00:04:15 Speaker 3 (Priya): No problem.
00:04:20 Speaker 3 (Priya): On the throughput side: when we introduced a synthetic adversarial long-tail workload (heavy multi-turn), baseline p99s spiked beyond 1.5s and caused queue buildup. Redwood's routing and admission control kept latencies bounded by shedding low-priority requests and rerouting them to fallback with graceful degradation — user-perceivable slowdown but no queue death.
00:04:44 Speaker 5 (Omar): Did you test network-induced jitter? Our egress across the peering link can be noisy at certain times.
00:04:50 Speaker 3 (Priya): We added jitter of +/-50ms to subset runs; Redwood's batching scheduler is resilient — p95 only moved by about 10-12% under that jitter. Baseline showed much larger sensitivity.
00:05:05 Speaker 2 (Carlos): On cost — what's the per-1M token delta for this config? We need ballpark economics to share with procurement.
00:05:12 Speaker 1 (Liam): Short answer: for the dedicated 4-slot quantized profile, Redwood unit cost is roughly 35-40% lower than CloudX for steady-state. The AE note: I'll follow up with a clearer pricing sheet that shows dedicated commit vs hosted burst math.
00:05:28 Speaker 6 (Leah): Do you have an estimate for peak burst costs? We won't commit to a big reserved pool until we see stable savings.
00:05:34 Speaker 1 (Liam): We can do month-to-month reserved slots with burst credits; I'll put the options side-by-side in the sheet.
00:05:40 Speaker 3 (Priya): Quick note on model artifacts — we tracked tokenization differences. Some of the delta at short prompts was due to different tokenizers or how the baseline truncates. We normalized that but there are still edge cases.
00:05:56 Speaker 4 (Ruth): Can we get the exact prompt list and the two raw traces for one failing example? That will help our NLU folks debug.
00:06:04 Speaker 3 (Priya): Yes — I'll upload CSVs and a small trace bundle to the shared folder.
00:06:09 Speaker 5 (Omar): Regarding private deployments — we still need an estimate for a VPC private plane — you mentioned a private control plane option earlier. Does that change perf?
00:06:19 Speaker 3 (Priya): Private control plane mainly affects management path. Data plane performance is the same if we colocate in your VPC. There is slight overhead if the customer enforces additional egress inspection, but Redwood runtime is optimized for minimal RTT.
00:06:33 Speaker 2 (Carlos): What's the timeline to switch a canary on production? We want a conservative cutover: canary to 1% then 5% then 25% over two weeks.
00:06:41 Speaker 1 (Liam): Sounds reasonable. Our rollout flags are built-in — you can control by token or user-id, and we can do automatic rollback if latency thresholds or quality regressions cross thresholds. We'll need some runbook approvals from your SREs though.
00:06:58 Speaker 6 (Leah): On the subject of SLOs — what verification do you need from our side to agree go/no-go?
00:07:06 Speaker 3 (Priya): Ideally: (1) latency p95 under 500ms for the production mix, (2) accuracy delta <1% on our eval suite, (3) no sustained error-rate increase or queue saturation for 72h at ramp levels. Those are negotiable but are what we typically measure.
00:07:23 Speaker 2 (Carlos): That p95 number is doable based on today's numbers. Ruth, Omar — any objection?
00:07:29 Speaker 4 (Ruth): From ML side, we want the flagged 4 prompts re-run with fp16 to confirm it's quantization-related before we accept a rollout.
00:07:36 Speaker 3 (Priya): Yes, will run both quant and fp16 for those 4.
00:07:40 Speaker 5 (Omar): Omar: I'll need a short maintenance window to enable peering logs and grant the test IAM role. Would prefer before Monday.
00:07:48 Speaker 1 (Liam): Ok noted.
00:07:50 Speaker 3 (Priya): Switching gears — routing policy specifics. We propose primary -> dedicated slot pool in us-east-1, fallback -> hosted us-east-1, and emergency -> baseline (CloudX) but only if flagged by request label "legacy-allow". That keeps us in control and avoids silent cross-provider swings.
00:08:09 Speaker 2 (Carlos): That label approach seems fine. How do we instrument the rollback triggers?
00:08:14 Speaker 3 (Priya): We can tie to three signals: p95 above threshold, error-rate above 0.5%, and quality regression delta from on-the-fly evals. If any two signals hit, automatic rollback. We also surface alerts to your SRE Slack channel.
00:08:29 Speaker 6 (Leah): Will that on-the-fly eval use a shadowed copy of traffic? Does it affect throughput?
00:08:34 Speaker 3 (Priya): It's sampled — 0.5-1% of traffic for eval hooks. Minimal perf impact; we run evaluations asynchronously.
00:08:43 Speaker 4 (Ruth): Curious — in your tests how often did admission control kick in? Were requests dropped or queued?
00:08:49 Speaker 3 (Priya): In one synthetic spike run, admission control shed about 6% of low-priority requests and routed 12% to hosted fallback. No client errors — just increased tail for low-priority.
00:09:01 Speaker 5 (Omar): For the shed policy, can we define which endpoints or customers are low priority? We need flexibility.
00:09:07 Speaker 1 (Liam): Yes you can configure by route tag, API key, or token metadata. We'll work with Omar to map existing routing tags.
00:09:16 Speaker 2 (Carlos): Another question — does the dedicated pool autoscale? We don't want manual interventions at 3am.
00:09:23 Speaker 3 (Priya): Autoscaling is available with guardrails; scale actions are based on queue lengths and observed p95; ramp limits and cooldowns are configurable. For reserved capacity, you can choose immediate scale only within burst credits.
00:09:36 Speaker 6 (Leah): On the security front, we need SOC2 Type II and a data processing addendum. Where do we sign?
00:09:43 Speaker 1 (Liam): I'll attach our compliance bundle and DPA in the follow-up. Legal typically does a quick review; we have existing templates for enterprise.
00:09:51 Speaker 4 (Ruth): Slight transcribe note — earlier you said "Argenta" — Ruth again — that's totally fine.
00:09:55 Speaker 3 (Priya): heh, yeah captured that.
00:09:58 Speaker 3 (Priya): Now quick deep-dive numbers for the flagged prompts. Prompt A shows p95 1.8s on baseline and 1.1s on Redwood quant; confidence dropped from 0.92 to 0.86 on quant. When we switch to fp16 Q95 drops to 1.05s and confidence restores to 0.91. So quantization is the likely culprit.
00:10:22 Speaker 4 (Ruth): Good — that aligns with our hypothesis. Please include the trace for Prompt A.
00:10:27 Speaker 3 (Priya): Will do.
00:10:30 Speaker 5 (Omar): Regarding network peering — any changes required on our side to support the private control plane?
00:10:36 Speaker 3 (Priya): Peering config is standard: VPC peering or PrivateLink depending on your infra; you'll need to open few egress ports and allow our egress IPs. I'll share the minimal firewall rule set.
00:10:47 Speaker 2 (Carlos): On the artifact side — can you consolidate the artifacts? We want: (1) the 10k head-to-head CSV, (2) per-request traces for the 4 failing prompts, (3) pricing sheet, (4) routing policy draft.
00:10:58 Speaker 1 (Liam): Yes — Priya and I will drop a zip into the shared drive with those items by Friday.
00:11:04 Speaker 6 (Leah): For our internal execs, can you provide a 1-pager that shows latency delta, cost delta, and risk summary?
00:11:10 Speaker 1 (Liam): We'll do that. Liam: assign one-pager.
00:11:14 Speaker 3 (Priya): Quick aside: we noticed memory fragmentation on a small subset of runs when using aggressive quant + long sequences. We patched runtime to reclaim KV pages more frequently; we'll include the patched binary and instructions.
00:11:29 Speaker 5 (Omar): Are those patches backward compatible with our current model?
00:11:33 Speaker 3 (Priya): Yes, no model change needed. It's a runtime GC tweak.
00:11:37 Speaker 2 (Carlos): Any limitations we should call out before signoff?
00:11:41 Speaker 3 (Priya): Two caveats: (1) extremely long context >8k still shows degraded perf for quantized runtimes, we recommend fp16 for those; (2) tokenization mismatches can cause nominal throughput variance — we can standardize tokenizers in the pilot.
00:11:57 Speaker 4 (Ruth): For the tokenizer standardization — can you pin to a single tokenizer version in the pilot?
00:12:02 Speaker 3 (Priya): Yes we'll pin it for the pilot, and include migration steps if you later switch.
00:12:08 Speaker 5 (Omar): Quick ops question: what logs do you need to debug live issues? Full request traces or sampled?
00:12:15 Speaker 3 (Priya): We ask for sampled full traces and aggregated metrics. For production incidents we can ask for full traces under an NDA if needed.
00:12:24 Speaker 2 (Carlos): Ok — looks like we have alignment on tests and next steps. Anything else?
00:12:29 Speaker 6 (Leah): One more — can you include a cost sensitivity chart: if p95 target relaxes from 400ms to 600ms, how cost changes?
00:12:36 Speaker 1 (Liam): Yes — we'll include a sensitivity chart.
00:12:40 Speaker 3 (Priya): I'll run the skewed 85/15 short/long test, the fp16 re-runs for the flagged 4 prompts, the network jitter tests at peak QPS, and then upload artifacts.
00:12:53 Speaker 5 (Omar): I'll stand up the test role and peering access today.
00:12:58 Speaker 1 (Liam): Perfect. Recap of next steps — Priya run 10k skewed and fp16 checks (due 2026-09-28), Omar provide access/logs (due 2026-09-25), Liam send pricing and 1-pager (due 2026-09-29). We'll reconvene next Wednesday same time to review the updated head-to-head.
00:13:18 Speaker 2 (Carlos): Works for us. Thanks team.
00:13:21 Speaker 4 (Ruth): Thanks.
00:13:23 Speaker 6 (Leah): Thanks all.
00:13:25 Speaker 3 (Priya): Thanks everyone.
00:13:28 Speaker 1 (Liam): End.

Notes/Artifacts referenced:
- Head-to-head CSV (10k requests) — will be uploaded to shared drive
- Per-request traces for flagged prompts A-D
- Pricing comparison sheet (dedicated vs hosted vs baseline)
- Routing policy draft and rollback thresholds

Transcription quirks: occasional speaker label swaps, "Argenta" instead of "Argentia", "K-V cache" sometimes transcribed as "K V cache". Some filler words and interruptions remain in place to preserve authenticity.

End of transcript.
